summary: Inside the Praetorium, Pilate’s soldiers dress Jesus as a mock king, crown Him with thorns, hail Him, strike Him and spit on Him.
key_insight: The soldiers staged a coronation as a joke: a robe, a crown, a scepter, a royal salute and bended knees. Without knowing it, they acted out the truth. Mark even says that, bowing the knee, “they worshiped Him.”
story: Pilate had handed Jesus over to be crucified. The governor’s soldiers took Him into the Praetorium {Mt} and called together the whole garrison.
They stripped Him {Mt} and clothed Him with purple. {Mk} They twisted a crown of thorns and put it on His head, and they put a reed in His right hand. {Mt}

Then they bowed the knee before Him and mocked Him: “Hail, King of the Jews!” They struck Him with their hands. {Jn} They spat on Him, took the reed and struck Him on the head with it. {Mt} And bowing the knee, they worshiped Him. {Mk}
differences: Matthew calls the robe scarlet; Mark and John call it purple.
Only Matthew mentions the reed placed in Jesus’ right hand. Matthew and Mark say the soldiers struck His head with the reed; John says they struck Him with their hands.
Matthew and Mark place the mockery after Pilate’s sentence. John places the crown of thorns and the purple robe before Pilate brings Jesus out, saying, “Behold the Man!” (John 19:5).
Matthew and Mark say the whole garrison was gathered. Only Mark says “they worshiped Him.”

fit.question: Was the robe scarlet (Matthew) or purple (Mark and John)?

points.label: A soldier’s cloak
points.text: The robe was most likely a Roman soldier’s red cloak, the nearest thing to royal dress in a barracks. A faded scarlet cloak could easily pass for a king’s purple in a mock coronation.

points.label: Words for color
points.text: Ancient color words covered a range. “Purple” named a family of costly reddish dyes. Matthew names the garment’s color; Mark and John name what it was meant to be: royal purple.

fit.note: The witnesses agree on the robe and the mockery; they differ only in naming its shade.
fit.short: It was probably a soldier’s red cloak. Matthew names its color, scarlet; Mark and John name what it stood for, royal purple.

fit.question: Matthew and Mark tell of the mockery after Pilate’s sentence. John places the crown of thorns and the robe before Pilate shows Jesus to the crowd. When did it happen?

points.label: Begun before, renewed after
points.text: McGarvey and others hold that the soldiers began mocking Jesus during the trial, at His scourging (John), and that once He was condemned and handed back to them, the whole garrison gathered and the mockery was renewed (Matthew, Mark).

points.label: Told together
points.text: Others think Matthew and Mark, having mentioned the scourging with the sentence, gather the soldiers’ abuse into one scene after it without fixing exactly when each part happened.

fit.note: John fixes the crown and robe before the verdict, and nothing in Matthew or Mark rules out an earlier start. The accounts can be read together without strain.
fit.short: The soldiers likely began mocking Jesus at His scourging (John) and renewed it with the whole garrison after the sentence (Matthew, Mark).

scene.label: The governor’s soldiers
scene.text: Pilate’s troops were auxiliaries, not legionaries from Italy. Josephus says they were recruited largely from non-Jewish cities of the region such as Caesarea and Sebaste in Samaria. Many despised the Jews, so mocking a “King of the Jews” let them mock the whole nation.

scene.label: A crown and a salute
scene.text: No one knows which thorny plant was used; several grow around Jerusalem. The crown mimicked the wreaths rulers wore, and “Hail, King of the Jews!” copied the soldiers’ salute to the emperor.

scene.label: Shame and spitting
scene.text: Isaiah’s Servant says, “I gave My back to those who struck Me,” and “I did not hide My face from shame and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6). Jesus had told the Twelve that the Gentiles would mock Him, scourge Him and spit on Him (Mark 10:34).

witnesses.matthew: Gives the fullest picture of a mock coronation: the scarlet robe, the crown, the reed in the right hand for a scepter, the kneeling. Matthew’s Gospel opened with Gentile wise men seeking the one “born King of the Jews” (2:2); now Gentile soldiers hail Him by that title in scorn.
witnesses.mark: Ends the scene with the startling words “they worshiped Him.” Jesus had foretold exactly this treatment (Mark 10:34). Soldiers of Rome mock the King whom a Roman centurion will soon confess as the Son of God (15:39).
witnesses.luke: Does not record this mockery by Pilate’s soldiers. He tells instead how Herod and his soldiers mocked Jesus and dressed Him in a gorgeous robe (Luke 23:11).
witnesses.john: Places the crown and the purple robe in the middle of the trial, so Jesus comes out wearing them when Pilate says, “Behold the Man!” The soldiers’ joke becomes Pilate’s exhibit, and John invites the reader to look at the crowned King.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the true King. He let soldiers dress Him as a joke, strike Him and spit on Him, and He did not revile them in return (1 Peter 2:23).
seeing.living: The soldiers bowed the knee in mockery; one day “every knee should bow” in truth (Philippians 2:10). Kneeling to Jesus on Sunday while living as if He were not King is its own kind of mockery. Give Him in daily obedience the honor the soldiers only pretended to give.
seeing.ponder: Is your worship of Jesus true honor, or a show that does not change how you live?

preaching.big_idea: The King crowned with thorns is the King God has crowned with glory and honor.
outline: A garrison gathered against one Man (27)
A King struck and spat upon (30)
preaching.watch_for: Each act of mockery copies an act of homage: robe, crown, scepter, salute, kneeling. The title “King of the Jews” frames Matthew’s Gospel, from the wise men who came to worship (2:2) to the charge nailed over the cross (27:37).
